response.title: Is a battery power station better than a computer battery backup for keeping the internet on during long outages?
response.answer:
Yes. For keeping your internet running during long power outages, a portable battery power station is generally better than a traditional computer battery backup (UPS).

However, there's an important trade-off:

UPS (Uninterruptible Power Supply): Better for keeping your internet running without interruption when electricity goes out.

Portable power station: Better for keeping your internet running for many hours or even days.

For home internet, the ideal solution may actually be a combination of both.

1. Battery power station vs. UPS

These runtimes are illustrative, not guaranteed. They depend heavily on the equipment's power consumption and battery capacity.

2. How long could a power station keep your internet running?

Assuming your modem, router, and fiber ONT (if present) together consume 25 watts, here are approximate runtimes.

Internet backup runtime calculator

Estimates assume 85% usable battery energy and 8 W of AC inverter overhead.

500 Wh — medium
1,000 Wh — large
2,000 Wh — extra large

Estimated runtime

12.9 hours

Actual runtime depends on the power station and load.

For low-power networking equipment, inverter efficiency and idle consumption matter a lot. A power station with a DC output matching your equipment can sometimes last substantially longer than one using AC outlets.

3. What I would recommend
Shop

Best for outages lasting 8–12 hours

A compact 250–500 Wh LiFePO4 power station with automatic backup switching. For example, the EcoFlow RIVER 3 Plus offers a manufacturer-rated transfer time under 10 ms. 
PowerStationGearLab
+1

Shop

Best for outages lasting 24+ hours

A roughly 1,000 Wh LiFePO4 power station, such as an Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2. Particularly useful if you also need to charge phones and laptops.

4. Two important things to watch out for

Automatic switching: Not every power station can function as a UPS. Some require manual activation after an outage, while others briefly interrupt power. EcoFlow's documentation, for example, distinguishes 10 ms and 20 ms backup modes. 
NFM
 Look for UPS/EPS functionality, AC pass-through support, and test that your router stays online during a simulated outage.

Your internet provider must also have power: Even if your modem and router remain powered, your connection could go down if the ISP's neighborhood equipment loses electricity. This is particularly relevant for cable internet. Fiber may be more resilient, depending on the provider's infrastructure.

One question that would change my recommendation

What type of home internet do you have?

Fiber (AT&T Fiber, Frontier, Verizon Fios, etc.)
Cable (Spectrum, Xfinity, Cox, etc.)
Starlink
Other / Not sure
Recommend my backup setup

This matters because fiber, cable, and Starlink have very different power requirements and outage characteristics.

## 1. Battery power station vs. UPS

| Feature | Computer UPS | Portable power station |
|---|---|---|
| Primary purpose | Short-term backup | Long-duration backup |
| Typical runtime for internet equipment | 1–5 hours | 8–48+ hours |
| Battery capacity | Usually smaller | Usually much larger |
| Instant power switching | Yes | Depends on model |
| Battery chemistry | Often lead-acid | Often LiFePO4 |
| Solar recharging | Usually no | Often supported |
| Cost per Wh of storage | Often higher | Often lower |
| Best use | Brief outages | Extended outages |

These runtimes are illustrative, not guaranteed. They depend heavily on the equipment's power consumption and battery capacity.

## 2. How long could a power station keep your internet running?

Assuming your modem, router, and fiber ONT (if present) together consume **25 watts**, here are approximate runtimes.

{@body const [watts,setWatts] = DIL.useState(25)}
{@body const [capacity,setCapacity] = DIL.useState("500")}
{@body const hours = Math.round((Number(capacity)*0.85/(watts+8))*10)/10}

  <text weight="medium">Internet backup runtime calculator</text>

      **{watts} W**
    </row>
    <slider min={10} max={80} step={5} value={watts} onChange={setWatts}/>
  </box>
  <box gap={1}>
    <label>Power station battery capacity</label>
    <radio-group direction="col" value={capacity} onChange={setCapacity}>
      <radio value="250">250 Wh — small</radio>
      <radio value="500">500 Wh — medium</radio>

    <text color="secondary" size="xs">Actual runtime depends on the power station and load.</text>
  </box>
</box>

For low-power networking equipment, inverter efficiency and idle consumption matter a lot. A power station with a DC output matching your equipment can sometimes last substantially longer than one using AC outlets.

## 3. What I would recommend

    </box>

## 4. Two important things to watch out for

**Automatic switching:** Not every power station can function as a UPS. Some require manual activation after an outage, while others briefly interrupt power. **Your internet provider must also have power:** Even if your modem and router remain powered, your connection could go down if the ISP's neighborhood equipment loses electricity. This is particularly relevant for cable internet. Fiber may be more resilient, depending on the provider's infrastructure.
